name: Iran
headline: Iranians can see insurer prescription records, but there is no data protection law, and in January 2026 security forces reportedly tracked protesters through hospital records.

access.summary: A 2009 ministerial charter, not a statute, says patients may see their whole clinical record and get a copy. Insurer apps show prescription and treatment history, but no national patient portal to the full record was verified.
detail: The Patient Rights Charter, sent to health facilities by the health minister in Aban 1388 (late 2009), says a patient may access all information in their clinical record, receive a copy and ask for errors to be corrected. The clause sets no deadline.

The 2004 Electronic Commerce Law says a person must have access to computer files holding their personal data and may correct or erase wrong data. Article 60 sends medical records to a separate bylaw, which was not verified.

The head of the Iran Health Insurance Organization said in July 2026 that its app and a citizen system let all insured people view their treatment and insurance records. Usage figures were not verified.
Score: base 45 for a right with no national record portal, plus 5 for officially described insurer portals, minus 5 for no deadline and minus 5 because the right rests on a charter, not a law.

control.summary: The 2024 Seventh Plan Law makes every provider send health data to a central state database in real time. No patient opt-out or access log was found, and a UN report says security forces seized hospital admission lists in January 2026.
detail: Article 69 of the Seventh Development Plan Law (2024) requires all public, charity and private providers to send Iranians' health data online, at the time of service, to the National Health Database. Licence renewals depend on it.
The same article lets the ministry share that data with treating doctors and anyone allowed by law, or with the citizen's permission. The broad legal route leaves the patient little say.
The Sixth Plan Law (2017) said the national record should be built with privacy and subject to people's permission. No consent screen, opt-out or patient-visible access log was verified.
A UN Special Rapporteur report of March 2026 found that security forces searched wards room by room and seized patient admission lists during the protests.

privacy.summary: Iran has no general data protection law or regulator; a bill has been stalled for years. Health secrecy rests on the penal code and the e-commerce law, while the UN and the BBC report security forces using hospital records to find protesters.
detail: Article 58 of the Electronic Commerce Law bans electronic processing of data on physical, mental or sexual condition without explicit consent, and Article 71 sets one to three years in prison. Penal Code Article 648 punishes doctors and pharmacists who disclose secrets outside legal cases.

A personal data protection bill has been debated for years. Donya-e-Eqtesad reported in January 2025 that its fate and a rival parliament bill were still unclear. Passage by October 2026 was not verified.
Health workers told the BBC in January 2026 that security forces watched medical records to identify injured protesters. The UN Special Rapporteur documented hospital raids in 14 provinces.
The same report says a user privacy directive from the national cyberspace authority was issued about a year earlier, but its enforcement remained unclear.

commercial.summary: The e-commerce law requires explicit consent before health data is processed electronically and limits use to stated purposes, with prison for breaches. No rules on health data brokers, advertising or sale of de-identified data were found.
detail: Article 58 of the Electronic Commerce Law makes storing, processing or distributing health data messages without explicit consent unlawful. Article 59 limits data to stated purposes and what is necessary.
Article 71 sets one to three years in prison for breaching these rules. No prosecution for selling health data was verified.
No law or regulation on health data brokers, health apps or de-identified data sales was found.

In 2023 a Telegram channel claimed to have hacked about 20 insurance companies and offered their data for sale, BBC Persian reported. The central insurance regulator denied its own systems were hacked.

journey.summary: E-prescribing has run nationwide since early 2022 and logs about 600,000 prescriptions a day, linking doctors, pharmacies and insurers. A full national health record is still not in place, and the first vice president said in December 2025 that e-health lags the world average.
detail: The government daily Iran reported in August 2025 that e-prescribing reached the whole country from Dey 1400 (early 2022), but the health system still lacked an electronic health record. The minister promised one by March 2026.
The Iran Health Insurance Organization said in July 2026 that about 500 million e-prescriptions had been issued, about 220 million a year, and paper booklets were abolished.

SEPAS, the ministry's national record system, is meant to integrate citizens' health data nationwide. The Seventh Plan gives the ministry two years from 2024 to connect hospital, prescribing, primary care and self-care systems.
First Vice President Aref said in December 2025 that Iran is behind even the world average in e-health. An e-health roadmap was issued in October 2025.

clinical.summary: The law tells the health ministry to give treating doctors the data held in the national health database. Whether clinicians can actually pull a patient's history from other providers at the bedside was not verified, and the full national record is not finished.
detail: Tehran University of Medical Sciences describes SEPAS as a record from before birth to after death that gives people involved in care access to patients' electronic files.
Article 69 of the Seventh Plan Law requires the ministry to make stored data available to treating doctors, and to others allowed by law or by the citizen.
Official and press reports through 2025 say the national record is still incomplete. No figures on clinician lookups across providers were found.

research.summary: A national ethics committee issues ethics approval codes that journals check online, and the patient charter gives a right to refuse research. No general opt-out or public register of data uses was found.
detail: The Patient Rights Charter says patients may choose whether to take part in any research without it affecting their care, and must be told of any research procedures.

Journal articles must carry an ethics approval code registered in the National Committee for Ethics in Biomedical Research system, where each code can be checked online. National guidelines, reviewed in a 2019 paper, cover consent, confidentiality, trials and use of health data.

Whether registry or record data are used for research without consent was not verified. Score: base 40, plus 3 for an ethics body and 3 for statutory secrecy (Penal Code Article 648), held at 45, the lower half of the band, because the key fact is unverified.

ai.summary: No binding rule for clinical AI is in force. The food and drug authority was reviewing a draft instruction for registering medical software, including AI, in May 2026, and a health-sector AI document is still being drafted.
detail: In April 2026 an adviser to the Iran Food and Drug Administration described a three-part AI strategy, including oversight of AI-based products and a sandbox for testing them.

In May 2026 the authority's medical devices office reviewed a draft instruction for registering medical device software, which it said would assess technical, clinical and security documents. Final adoption and any change control rules were not verified.
Tehran University of Medical Sciences said in October 2025 that a national AI document exists, but a separate health-sector AI document is being drafted.
